analysis.one_liner: Bars U.S. trade pressure on poor countries' efforts to get cheap HIV/AIDS medicines.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees without a hearing or vote after being referred on the day it was introduced in July 2000.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed U.S. agencies to push drug companies and developing countries to make HIV/AIDS medicines available free or cheap in poor countries, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. It would have banned U.S. agencies from spending money to pressure those countries to weaken laws that promote drug access, barred the U.S. Trade Representative from bringing World Trade Organization cases against such laws, and had the President seek an exemption for developing countries from global patent rules that block cheap HIV/AIDS drugs. It was referred to two House committees and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with HIV/AIDS in developing countries, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, who would gain access to lower-cost medicines and medical technologies. Their governments would also gain room to use generic imports and other access policies without facing U.S. trade retaliation [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs Treasury, USAID, the U.S. Trade Representative, and the FDA to encourage drug companies to make HIV/AIDS medicines and technologies available in developing countries free or at prices tied to income levels [S2][S3].
It bars U.S. agencies from spending money to pressure developing countries to repeal or revise intellectual property or competition laws that promote access to HIV/AIDS drugs [S2][S3].
It prohibits the U.S. Trade Representative from initiating World Trade Organization proceedings against any developing country's law or policy that promotes access to HIV/AIDS medicines [S2][S3].

It directs the President to seek an exemption for developing countries, including all sub-Saharan African countries, from international patent rules (the WTO TRIPS agreement) that would restrict laws promoting access to HIV/AIDS medicines [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would bear the cost if it passed: they would lose the ability to use U.S. trade negotiations and WTO complaints to enforce patent protections on HIV/AIDS drugs in poor countries, and would face government pressure to cut prices or donate medicines [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's main tools are directives to 'encourage' other agencies and companies to act; it creates no enforcement mechanism, so its practical impact on drug prices would depend on voluntary compliance [S2][S3].

By seeking exemptions from patent rules for AIDS drugs in poor countries, the bill would shrink patent-protected sales there, which the pharmaceutical industry argues are part of the revenue that funds research into new medicines [S3].

Barring U.S. WTO challenges would limit one of the government's standard trade-enforcement tools, which trade officials could argue weakens America's bargaining position across trade agreements more broadly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and enormous problem — HIV/AIDS drugs priced far beyond the reach of patients in the world's poorest countries, while the U.S. government's trade machinery pushed those countries to enforce patents. Its cost to drug companies would be confined to poor-country markets, where sales were already minimal, and its benefit to patients was potentially large. Its main weakness is that much of it is hortatory: it encourages rather than requires, so its direct effect would have been limited even if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and International Relations committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on July 27, 2000, with 11 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
On introduction day it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the International Relations Committee, the standard first step for a bill [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind; the record shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote [S5].
It finished with 20 cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies were better off: the bill's death left U.S. trade pressure and WTO enforcement intact to protect their patents on HIV/AIDS drugs in developing countries, and patients in those countries got no new access provisions from Congress.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing U.S. agencies to encourage affordable HIV/AIDS medicines in poor countries and to stop pressuring those countries over drug patents [S1][S3].

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee and 10 other original cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors (all Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction [S3][S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 106th Congress by Rep. Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral; the record shows no committee action [S5].

against.name: House International Relations Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 106th Congress by Rep. Benjamin Gilman (R-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; the record shows no committee action [S5].

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry whose patent revenue and trade leverage the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Widely reported to have campaigned during this period against developing-country access laws, including a lawsuit against South Africa's medicines law, and to have pressed U.S. officials to defend global patent rules — the exact pressure this bill would have banned.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent (Bernie Sanders); no Republican signed on, and the two committees that buried the bill were both chaired by Republicans [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have barred the U.S. government from using trade negotiations and WTO complaints to defend the companies' patents on HIV/AIDS drugs in poor countries, and would have pressured them to cut prices or donate medicines there. Their interest in keeping those tools ran against the access needs of patients in poor countries [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Generic drug makers (India, Brazil, and other producing countries)
industries.note: Exempting developing countries from patent rules that block cheap HIV/AIDS medicines would open space for generic competition in those markets, which is how prices for AIDS drugs were eventually driven down.
